payload.throughline: Build nucleic acids from nucleotide structure, use complementarity to match strands, then trace replication, chromosome-end maintenance, and sequence repair.

learner_content_blocks: Starting check: distinguish a sugar-plus-base nucleoside from a phosphate-bearing nucleotide. This is low stakes and does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: move from monomer parts to polymer organization. Identify sugar, phosphate, and base; then decide whether a feature belongs to the repeating backbone or projects from it.

A nucleoside is a pentose sugar joined to a nitrogenous base. Adding one or more phosphate groups produces a nucleotide. During polymer formation, phosphodiester bonds connect the sugar of one residue to the phosphate associated with the next, creating a repeating sugar-phosphate backbone.

The nitrogenous bases project from the backbone. Purines have a fused two-ring framework; pyrimidines have one ring. DNA commonly contains deoxyribose and thymine, whereas RNA contains ribose and uracil. These shared categories matter more here than memorizing one isolated KC for each base.
Mental model — Parts: sugar + base = nucleoside; add phosphate = nucleotide. Polymer: repeat sugar-phosphate along the chain while base residues project from each sugar.

Expert selection: I first locate phosphate. If phosphate is absent, I am looking at a nucleoside; if present, a nucleotide is possible. On a polymer, I trace the repeating sugar-phosphate path and treat the attached rings as base residues. I rule out a base-to-base backbone because the bases are side groups, not the repeating chain.

Worked example: a diagram shows ribose attached to adenine and a phosphate, followed by another ribose-phosphate unit. The first residue is a nucleotide because all three components are present. The repeating path alternates sugar and phosphate; adenine is a projecting purine residue. For a supplied DNA coding strand written 5′→3′, the information-preserving RNA keeps that order, replaces T with U, and uses ribose instead of deoxyribose.
Guided practice: trace the continuous sugar-phosphate path before classifying the attached base ring.
Less help: classify a fresh monomer and decide which component becomes part of the repeating polymer backbone.
On your own: use the supplied coding-strand direction, preserve its base order, replace thymine with uracil, and identify ribose as the RNA sugar.

Boundary: a base residue is attached to the backbone but is not itself the repeating backbone. Complementary pairing between bases is taught in the next KC; this KC focuses on composition and polymer organization.
Near exit: identify a purine residue and its relationship to the sugar-phosphate backbone in a fresh polymer diagram.
Changed-task exit: predict the structural consequence of cleaving a phosphodiester linkage rather than altering a base residue.
Repair the failed near-use function: trace the repeating sugar-phosphate chain, then classify the attached one-ring or two-ring base. Do not place the base in the backbone.
Fresh near-use re-entry: classify a new RNA residue and locate its projecting pyrimidine without reusing the exposed diagram.
Repair the failed changed-task function: name which component or bond changed, then ask whether the change interrupts chain continuity or only changes the identity of a side-group base.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: predict the result of removing a backbone phosphate from a new short polymer segment.
Recap: nucleoside equals sugar plus base; nucleotide adds phosphate. Nucleic acids repeat a sugar-phosphate backbone and carry projecting purine or pyrimidine residues.
If one fresh re-entry remains unresolved, return to the planner without exit credit and resume later at the exact failed structural function.
Starting check: pair one DNA base with its Watson–Crick partner. This is low stakes and does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: use base-pair specificity and opposite strand orientations to match information, then apply the same rule when strands separate, reanneal, or hybridize.
In DNA, adenine pairs with thymine and guanine pairs with cytosine. The two strands run antiparallel, so a sequence written 5′ to 3′ aligns with its complement written 3′ to 5′.

Denaturation disrupts the noncovalent interactions that hold paired strands together while leaving each covalent sugar-phosphate backbone intact. When conditions permit, complementary strands can reanneal. Hybridization applies the same matching rule to strands from different molecules, including RNA where uracil substitutes for thymine.
This lesson uses sequence matching and strand-state logic, not advanced thermodynamic calculations.
Mental model — Keep each backbone intact, reverse the orientation, apply A–T or A–U and G–C matching, then count whether the required positions complement.

Expert selection: I write the orientation labels before pairing any bases. Then I align each template position with its specific partner. For a strand transition, I ask whether backbones stay intact and whether enough complementary positions remain to support pairing; I do not treat denaturation as nucleotide cleavage.

Worked example: the DNA strand 5′-AGTC-3′ pairs with 3′-TCAG-5′. Heating can separate those strands by disrupting interstrand interactions, but each sequence remains covalently connected. A strand 3′-TGAG-5′ contains one mismatch and is therefore a poorer information match. No melting-temperature calculation is needed.
Guided practice: label both ends, write the complement under each base, and check every aligned position.
Less help: identify which fresh strand can reanneal after separation using sequence and orientation alone.
On your own: distinguish strand separation from backbone cleavage and predict which information remains preserved.
Boundary: denaturation separates paired strands but does not hydrolyze the sugar-phosphate backbone. Similar base composition is not enough for hybridization when aligned bases are not complementary.
Near exit: construct the antiparallel complement of a fresh short DNA sequence.
Changed-task exit: select an RNA probe that hybridizes to a DNA target and predict how a single mismatch changes the match without calculating thermodynamics.
Repair the failed near-use function: write 5′ and 3′ labels first, then pair A with T and G with C at each aligned position.
Fresh near-use re-entry: build a new antiparallel DNA complement with no sequence family reused.
Repair the failed changed-task function: separate backbone integrity from interstrand pairing, substitute U for T in RNA, and inspect each aligned position for complementarity.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: evaluate a new RNA–DNA hybridization pair containing one changed target base.
Recap: preserve orientation, apply specific base pairing, and distinguish intact separated strands from cleaved polymers. Reannealing and hybridization require complementary information matching.
If one fresh re-entry remains unresolved, return to the planner without exit credit and resume later at the exact failed complementarity function.
Starting check: identify which strand can serve as a template after a DNA duplex separates. This is low stakes and does not select a route or establish mastery.

Goal: trace one complete replication logic chain—open the duplex, prime synthesis, extend complementary DNA, join discontinuous products, and identify the parental and new strands in each daughter molecule.

Replication begins at an origin. Helicase separates the parental strands, exposing templates. Primase supplies a short primer with a free 3′ end. DNA polymerase adds complementary DNA nucleotides to that end, so new DNA grows 5′ to 3′.

Because parental strands are antiparallel, one new strand can be extended toward the fork more continuously while the other is synthesized in pieces that are later joined by ligase. After copying, each daughter duplex contains one parental strand and one new strand: semiconservative replication.

A bacterial chromosome may use one main origin, whereas a long eukaryotic chromosome uses multiple origins so many segments can be copied at the same time. The target is this coordination, not an exhaustive replisome parts list.
Mental model — Origin → helicase opens → primer supplies 3′ end → polymerase extends 5′ to 3′ by complementarity → ligase seals discontinuities → one old plus one new strand per daughter.

Expert selection: I mark parental strands before following enzymes. If no primer exists, polymerase lacks the required starting 3′ end. If fragments are made but remain disconnected, I inspect ligase. For a long eukaryotic chromosome, I choose multiple origins when the issue is copying distant regions concurrently.

Worked example: helicase opens a duplex at an origin. A primer is placed on each exposed template, polymerase extends complementary DNA 5′ to 3′, and ligase seals adjacent fragments on the discontinuously synthesized strand. When the molecules separate, each daughter duplex contains one strand from the original duplex and one newly built strand. The process is semiconservative, not conservative or dispersive.
Guided practice: order origin opening, primer formation, polymerase extension, and ligase sealing before naming the daughter-strand composition.
Less help: locate the missing enzyme action from the first failed step in a fresh fork trace.
On your own: predict the daughter duplexes after one labelled parental strand is followed through replication.

Boundary: polymerase extends an existing 3′ end; it does not start a strand from nothing. Ligase seals adjacent DNA pieces; it does not unwind the parental duplex. Semiconservative describes strand ancestry, not the number of origins.
Near exit: identify the parental and newly synthesized strand in each daughter duplex.
Changed-task exit: predict how disabling most origins on a long eukaryotic chromosome changes the replication pattern while the remaining forks still function.
Repair the failed near-use function: label the two parental strands before synthesis, then follow each into a different daughter duplex and pair it with one new complement.
Fresh near-use re-entry: trace different parental labels through a new replication diagram.
Repair the failed changed-task function: find the earliest blocked action—opening, primer creation, extension, or sealing—and distinguish that local defect from origin number.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: evaluate a new multiple-origin chromosome after a primase defect at one origin.
Recap: origins organize starts; helicase opens, primase starts, polymerase extends by complementarity, and ligase seals. Each daughter duplex preserves one parental strand.
If one fresh re-entry remains unresolved, return to the planner without exit credit and resume later at the exact failed replication function.
Starting check: identify why polymerase needs an existing 3′ end. This is low stakes and does not select a route or establish mastery.
Goal: apply ordinary replication rules at the physical end of a linear chromosome and explain why that geometry creates a special maintenance problem.

DNA polymerase extends an existing 3′ end. On the discontinuously synthesized strand, primers are removed and internal gaps can be filled from an upstream DNA 3′ end. At the extreme chromosome end, removal of the final primer leaves no upstream 3′ end in the missing interval, so conventional polymerase cannot replace the terminal segment.

Repeated copying without specialized maintenance can therefore shorten chromosome ends. Telomerase uses its own RNA template to extend the chromosome's template end with repeat sequence, creating room for primer placement and additional conventional synthesis.

This is specialized maintenance of replicating linear DNA ends. It is distinct from the general logic used to correct an internal copying error or a mutation, and it does not require a catalogue of named repair pathways.
Mental model — Internal primer gap has an upstream 3′ end; terminal primer gap does not. Extend the template end first, then conventional synthesis can fill more of the complement.

Expert selection: I locate the extreme end and ask what 3′ end polymerase could extend after primer removal. If none exists, ordinary gap filling cannot solve it. I choose specialized end maintenance rather than general internal repair because the problem comes from chromosome geometry, not an isolated mismatched base.

Worked example: the final RNA primer on a newly made lagging strand is removed. The remaining gap lies at the physical end, with no upstream DNA 3′ end available inside the missing segment. Telomerase first lengthens the parental template end; a new primer can then be placed farther out, allowing polymerase to synthesize additional DNA. The chromosome may still retain terminal repeats rather than losing essential internal sequence.
Guided practice: mark the final primer, remove it, and identify whether an extendable 3′ end remains.
Less help: compare an internal primer gap with a terminal gap and choose which one conventional polymerase can fill.
On your own: predict the long-term consequence of repeated replication without specialized end maintenance.

Boundary: telomere maintenance addresses end-replication geometry; it is not the same task as correcting an internal mismatch or reversing every mutation. The target is introductory mechanism, not a named repair-pathway catalogue.
Near exit: explain why the final primer-removal gap cannot be filled by conventional polymerase alone.
Changed-task exit: predict chromosome-end behavior across repeated divisions when telomerase is inactive but internal replication and repair remain functional.
Repair the failed near-use function: draw the missing terminal segment and search specifically for an upstream 3′ end. If none exists, polymerase cannot initiate fill-in there.
Fresh near-use re-entry: analyze the opposite chromosome end in a new orientation without reusing the exposed diagram.
Repair the failed changed-task function: separate specialized end extension from internal error repair, then trace repeated cycles to a cumulative end-length consequence.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: predict how restored template-end extension changes a new cell-line scenario.
Recap: conventional polymerase needs a 3′ end, and the terminal primer gap lacks one. Specialized extension of the template end creates room for more conventional synthesis.
If one fresh re-entry remains unresolved, return to the planner without exit credit and resume later at the exact failed chromosome-end function.
Starting check: identify which intact strand can preserve sequence information when the other strand contains one altered base. This is low stakes and does not select a route or establish mastery.

Goal: explain repair by function rather than memorizing pathway names. Locate the defect, identify the intact information, remove or reverse the problem, replace missing DNA, and restore strand continuity.

During replication, polymerase can detect some incorrect additions and replace them before synthesis continues. Errors that remain or damage that occurs later can distort DNA or create an abnormal pairing pattern.

A general repair logic is: detect the abnormal feature, remove or chemically reverse the damaged or incorrect material, use an intact complementary strand as a template when available, synthesize replacement DNA, and seal the backbone. If a sequence change becomes fixed in both strands, the original information may no longer be recoverable from complementarity alone.

Chromosome-end maintenance is related to replication integrity but solves a terminal geometry problem. This KC addresses copying errors and DNA damage without importing a named repair-pathway catalogue.
Mental model — Detect → identify trustworthy template information → remove or reverse defect → replace by complementarity → seal → verify sequence and backbone.

Expert selection: I first ask when the defect appeared and whether one strand still preserves the expected information. A single mismatch after copying can often be corrected using the intact partner as a guide. If both strands carry the same altered pair, complementarity confirms the mutation rather than revealing the former sequence.

Worked example: a newly synthesized strand contains T opposite template G. The mismatch is detected before it becomes established in both strands. The incorrect T is removed, the intact G directs insertion of C, and the backbone is resealed. The reasoning depends on template information and ordered functions, not on recalling a pathway name.
Guided practice: identify the abnormal pair, choose the intact information source, and order removal, replacement, and sealing.
Less help: distinguish an incorrect newly added base from a damaged base on an older strand before predicting the repair template.
On your own: predict what remains unresolved when a defect is removed but replacement synthesis or sealing fails.

Boundary: repair is not guaranteed to recover an earlier sequence after a mutation is fixed on both strands. Telomere maintenance addresses a chromosome end, not a single internal mismatch. Named pathway catalogues are outside scope.
Near exit: order the functional steps that restore one mismatched base and backbone continuity.
Changed-task exit: compare a replication error caught immediately with damage detected after copying and decide which strand can serve as the information template.
Repair the failed near-use function: follow detect, remove, replace from intact complement, and seal. Do not credit removal alone as complete repair.
Fresh near-use re-entry: restore a different mismatch using a new strand and position.
Repair the failed changed-task function: mark defect timing and strand ancestry, then identify whether complementary information distinguishes the altered base from the intended one.
Fresh changed-task re-entry: analyze a new lesion that appears after replication and predict the consequence of losing replacement synthesis.
Recap: repair is a functional sequence—detect, use trustworthy information, remove or reverse, replace, seal, and verify. Timing and template availability determine what can be restored.
If one fresh re-entry remains unresolved, return to the planner without exit credit and resume later at the exact failed repair function.
